papers.title: A big picture perspective on narcolepsy and cardiovascular health: a plain language summary of publication.
Sleep quality moderating the relationship between hearing loss and cognition in older adults: Implications for Alzheimer's disease risk.
papers.abstract: BackgroundHearing impairment and poor sleep quality are prevalent, modifiable risk factors for cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease (AD), but their combined influence on cognition remains unclear.ObjectiveTo examine whether sleep quality modifies the association between hearing impairment and cognitive performance in older adults.MethodsData were drawn from 122 older adults in the MedWalk study. Peripheral hearing (pure-tone average), speech-in-noise (SiN), sleep quality (PSQI), and cognition (CANTAB) were assessed. Generalized linear models tested whether sleep quality moderated associations between hearing and cognition, adjusting for age, sex, and education.ResultsSleep quality moderated these associations, with effects differing by hearing type and cognitive domain. Poorer sleep quality strengthened the association between peripheral hearing loss and associative learning, with greater total errors (Exp(β) = 1.005, p = 0.010) and lower first attempt accuracy (Exp(β) = 0.998, p = 0.021). Poorer sleep quality also strengthened the association between poorer SiN performance and increased spatial working memory errors (Exp(β) = 1.009, p = 0.004) and slower reaction times (Exp(β) = 1.002, p = 0.031). A threshold effect emerged, with poor sleep quality associated with worse associative learning in individuals with moderate-or-greater peripheral hearing loss. Final stratified analysis showed a 15 dB increase in hearing loss was associated with 38.6% more associative learning errors among poor sleepers (PSQI > 5).ConclusionsFindings suggest hearing and sleep quality interact to affect cognition in domain specific ways that are relevant to AD risk. Prospective studies are needed to identify if joint interventions can reduce AD risk.Trial RegistrationThis study was registered with the Australian New Zealand Clinical trials Registry ACTRN12620000978965 (https://www.anzctr.org.au).

papers.title: Schizophrenia heterogeneity, treatment response to clozapine, and the Johns Hopkins Schizoaffective Disorders Precision Medicine Center of Excellence.
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia heterogeneity has resisted resolution for over a century, with no unifying clinical feature, biomarker, or pathogenic pathway identified. This has produced imprecise diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment, while confounding mechanistic research. Prior subtyping approaches-based on clinical phenotype, longitudinal course, age of onset, neuroimaging, physiological measures, or etiological factors-have yielded partial insights but lack established clinical utility. The Johns Hopkins Schizoaffective Disorder Precision Medicine Center of Excellence (PMCOE) brings together patients and clinicians at the Johns Hopkins Hospital and the Johns Hopkins Bayview Community Psychiatry Program with Johns Hopkins schizophrenia investigators to address this heterogeneity through stratification by treatment response, dividing patients into non-treatment-resistant (nonTRS), clozapine-responsive treatment-resistant (crTRS), and ultra-treatment-resistant (uTRS) subgroups. The term "Schizoaffective Disorder" was chosen to include schizophrenia with varying degrees of affective symptomatology, deliberately creating a broadly inclusive patient group. We hypothesize that these subtypes reflect distinct pathophysiological processes and that identifying their biological correlates will improve clinical decision-making and reveal novel therapeutic targets. The PMCOE pursues this hypothesis across four aims. Aim 1 characterizes clinical, cognitive, functional, quality-of-life, and olfactory signatures distinguishing subtypes, with preliminary data showing worse cognition and function in uTRS versus crTRS, and a temporal sequence of clozapine benefit (symptoms, then function, then quality of life). Aim 2 applies 7T structural/functional MRI-including novel measures of microvascular perfusion (iVASO) and CSF clearance (cDSC)-alongside EEG-based dynamic causal and network modeling to probe excitatory/inhibitory imbalance across subtypes. Aim 3 investigates cellular and molecular mechanisms, particularly protein homeostasis dysfunction, using patient-derived induced neurons, organoids, and extracellular vesicles, with focused study of SCHEMA-identified risk genes, including CUL1. Aim 4 leverages electronic health record data to generate validated electronic phenotypes for treatment-response subtypes and to establish a learning health system translating findings into clinical practice. By anchoring subtyping to an empirically measurable, clinically actionable outcome, the PMCOE aims to accelerate biomarker discovery for clozapine response, clarify mechanisms of treatment resistance, and transform care for individuals with schizophrenia-particularly those with ultra-treatment-resistant illness, for whom therapeutic options remain critically limited.

papers.title: Psychological well-being, sleep quality, physical activity, and work productivity in working and nonworking Jordanian women during Ramadan.
papers.abstract: BackgroundEmployed women are more likely to experience psychological distress such as depression, anxiety, and chronic stress, particularly in the absence of appropriate workplace supports and work-family balance policies.ObjectiveThe present study explored associations between psychological well-being, sleep quality, physical activity, health-related quality of life, and work productivity among working (WK) and nonworking (NWK) Jordanian women during Ramadan.MethodsA cross-sectional study of 1312 Jordanian women (529 working, 783 nonworking) was conducted in the Ramadan month using validated Arabic questionnaires (Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale (DASS-21), the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ-S), the Health Survey, and the Health and Work Questionnaire (HWQ).ResultsParticipants were mostly aged as >=35 years (57.0%), married (66.4%), and family member of 3-5 (57.4%). Most had diplomas (21.1%) or bachelor's degrees (52.8%). Compared with NWK peers, WK women reported significantly higher levels of depression, anxiety, and stress levels (all p < 0.001). Though, sleep quality and levels of physical activity were not significantly different between the groups. However, WK women had lower physical HRQoL scores (p = 0.028). Linear regression analysis (R2 = 0.25) showed that depression, stress, poor quality of sleep, and chronic disease were negative predictors of HRQoL, while work productivity and physical activity were positive predictors.ConclusionsWK Jordanian women are at significantly higher psychological distress and poorer physical health during Ramadan, with depression proving as the highest HRQoL determinant, highlighting the importance of gender sensitive workplace policies during Ramadan.

papers.title: Spectroscopic classification of non-ergodic populations.
papers.abstract: Non-ergodicity affects statistical inference in a diverse range of disciplines inside and outside physics. However, the concept of ergodicity is used inconsistently and may refer to several non-equivalent notions. To help address this, we first identify and clarify the relationship between three major interpretations of ergodicity. We then introduce a method of spectral analysis of non-ergodicity, which may be performed using data alone, and so may be applied in both numerical and empirical contexts. This may be used to identify, quantify and classify non-ergodic populations within an ergodic decomposition. This is demonstrated with an application to the Kob-Andersen (KA) kinetically constrained lattice glass model. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ergodicity and ergodicity breaking in the sciences'.
papers.journal: Philosophical transactions. Series A, Mathematical, physical, and engineering sciences

papers.title: Adolescent loneliness and health-compromising behaviors: Relations with dieting, substance use, and sleep disturbances.
papers.abstract: Loneliness is a major public health risk, and understanding its impacts on physical health is crucial for preventative healthcare strategies. This study examined whether adolescent loneliness predicted health-compromising behaviors (i.e. sleep disturbances, weight control, substance use) 1 year later and whether gender moderated these associations. Data were drawn from a longitudinal study of adolescents in the Southwestern United States (N = 751). Greater loneliness in ninth grade was associated with more frequent sleep disturbances 1 year later (an association that was significantly stronger among girls than boys) and with larger increases in sleep disturbances over the same period. Loneliness was not associated with dieting or substance use. Findings highlight loneliness as a contributor to adolescent sleep disturbances, particularly among girls, and a potential target for intervention.

papers.title: Electrifying diversity of the synaptic cleft.
papers.abstract: At synapses, the pre- and the postsynaptic cell are separated by a space of 10-50 nm wide called the synaptic cleft. Electric currents run through this synaptic cleft, particularly during synaptic transmission. Which types of currents, their size and their impact on synaptic transmission has only been systematically evaluated at a few synapses (1-5). Here, we highlight the electrical properties of the synaptic cleft. First, we discuss the subsynaptic distribution of different types of ion channels and their contribution to the cleft current. While the presence of capacitive, voltage-gated calcium, and ionotropic receptor currents at the cleft is uncontroversial, at many synapses voltage-gated potassium and sodium currents are excluded from the cleft. Second, we outline the biophysical relations between the cleft current and geometry, including the cleft potential profile and the cleft equivalent resistance, for four simplified synaptic geometries. Based on recent measurements and theory, cleft resistance does not vary dramatically, ranging between 0.5-40 MΩ for most synapses except for encapsulating synapses, whose resistance can be appreciably higher (up to 80 MΩ). Third, we demonstrate that discernable ephaptic transmission needs cleft currents surpassing 1 nA, or 500 pA for encapsulated synapses. Cleft potentials of a few millivolts may modulate synaptic transmission by changing gating of voltage-dependent channels. Fourth, we survey synaptopathies, in which dysfunctional cleft electrophysiology might be expected, yet evidence for such alterations is currently lacking. We conclude that despite its small size, the synaptic cleft is remarkably good at dissipating the currents that flow during synaptic transmission.

papers.title: Disentangling the mechanisms of aperiodic neural activity using pluripotent stem cell-derived neural tissue models.
papers.abstract: Neural field potentials contain periodic (rhythmic) and aperiodic (arrhythmic) activity patterns. Both carry physiological information that can be inferred from the shape of the power spectrum. The emergence of pluripotent stem cell (PSC)-derived neural tissue cultures and organoid technology has paved the way for quantifying, with unprecedented access, how aperiodic activity is shaped during the earliest points of cortical development. This review examines how a framework built historically from simulations and recordings from humans and animal models could be applied to neural tissue culture systems to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of aperiodic activity.

papers.title: Autistic Adolescents and Associate Medical Conditions.
papers.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder is a neurological and developmental condition impacting 1 in 31 children. Children, identified on the autism spectrum, are typically diagnosed by the age of 8; however, research indicates that there could be as many as 25% of undiagnosed adolescents. Autistic adolescents have a significantly higher prevalence of mental-health and medical conditions than their neurotypical peers including gastrointestinal disorders (e.g., chronic constipation), seizure disorders, sleep disturbances, and nutritional disorders (e.g., overeating). Part-1, "Interventions for Adolescent Students with Autism and Co-Occurring Mental Health Disorders," of this three-part series discussed interventions for the mental health comorbidities often experienced by autistic adolescents. This second article will address common medical conditions experienced by autistic adolescents and how school nurses can help manage these conditions in school settings.

papers.title: Specific associations of seven dimensions of sleep quality with suicide behaviours in Chinese adolescents: the partially moderating role of morning chronotype.
papers.abstract: To quantify the associations between seven dimensions of sleep quality and suicide behaviours (suicide ideation [SI], suicide plan [SP] and suicide attempt [SA]), and to examine the moderating role of chronotype in these relationships. A total of 20,055 adolescents were recruited through a stratified cluster sampling across 5 representative provinces in mainland China. Confounding variables included demographic characteristics, depression and anxiety. Among 20,055 adolescents, 2,099 had SI (10.5%), 1,596 had SP (7.9%) and 1,005 had SA (5.0%). In total, 4,276 were classified as morning-type (21.3%). Multinomial logistic regression analysis indicated that sleep duration and sleep disturbances were significantly associated with SI, SP and SA (all p < 0.05), whereas the relationship between subjective sleep quality and suicide behaviours was not significant (p > 0.05). Notably, hypnotic drug use is significantly associated only with SA (p < 0.05). Moreover, among morning-type adolescents, the relationships between the two dimensions of sleep quality (sleep disturbance and hypnotic drug use) and suicide behaviours became non-significant (p > 0.05). The seven dimensions of sleep quality exhibited unique associations with suicide behaviours in Chinese adolescents. Furthermore, morningness appears to partially moderate the associations between some sleep problems and suicide behaviours.

papers.title: Psychosocial stress in transitional societies: evidence from urbanising Eastern India.
papers.abstract: Small urban settlements are central to India's urban transition but remain underrepresented in research on perceived stress. This cross-sectional study examined perceived stress and its sociodemographic and behavioural correlates among 993 long-term adult residents of Bhawanipatna, Kesinga, Junagarh, and Dharamgarh in Kalahandi district, Odisha. Forty-nine of 58 municipal wards were selected by random draw; within those wards, eligible residents were recruited through in-person, mobile-telephone, and email contact. The author collected all data using a structured schedule that included the 10-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10). PSS-10 scores were low in 20.7%, moderate in 58.3%, and high in 20.9% of participants (mean 19.47, standard deviation (SD) 7.48). In a multivariable logistic regression model comparing moderate/high with low perceived stress, fruit and vegetable intake of at least five servings/day (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.05, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.03-0.10) and physical activity of at least 150 min/week (aOR 0.18, 95% CI 0.04-0.78) were associated with lower odds. Short sleep (aOR 7.29, 95% CI 1.66-32.10) and graduate-level education (aOR 2.37, 95% CI 1.18-4.73) were associated with higher odds. The results remained similar in two additional analyses: one that included study town and one that used Firth logistic regression for small groups. Because recruitment was not random at the individual level, the measures were self-reported, and the study was cross-sectional, the findings should not be interpreted as causal. The results show substantial perceived stress and strong links with reported health behaviours in this selected small-town sample. Representative longitudinal studies are needed to confirm them.

papers.title: Simulation in electrophysiology training: A needed new standard?
Dual-energy right atrial appendage tachycardia ablation in pediatrics.
Left Ventricular Hypertrophy with Ventricular Pre-Excitation: Distinguishing Sarcomeric Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy from Genetic and Metabolic Phenocopies.
papers.abstract: Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) accompanied by a short PR interval or ventricular pre-excitation should prompt consideration of diagnoses beyond conventional sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). This critical review examines the clinical, electrophysiologic, imaging, biochemical, genetic, and mechanistic features that distinguish sarcomeric HCM from PRKAG2 cardiomyopathy, Danon disease, and selected Fabry and Pompe disease phenocopies. Particular emphasis is placed on defining the electrical phenotype because a short PR interval, a true atrioventricular accessory pathway, and a fasciculoventricular pathway are not interchangeable findings. PRKAG2 cardiomyopathy combines autosomal dominant cardiac glycogenosis with variable hypertrophy, pre-excitation, atrial arrhythmias, and progressive conduction disease; emerging preclinical data also suggest early glycogen-independent AMPKγ2-myosin and calcium-handling abnormalities. Danon disease, caused by LAMP2 deficiency, is an aggressive X-linked cardioskeletal disorder in which fasciculoventricular and true atrioventricular accessory pathways may coexist, and phase 1 AAV9-LAMP2B gene-replacement data have now been reported. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance can refine the differential, including histologically validated low native T1 as a marker of myocardial glycosphingolipid accumulation in Fabry disease. A practical diagnostic strategy integrates the ECG mechanism, pedigree, extracardiac phenotype, echocardiography, cardiovascular magnetic resonance, disease-directed biochemical testing, genetic confirmation, and electrophysiology when pathway mechanism or risk remains uncertain. Correct molecular diagnosis directly changes surveillance, family screening, treatment, and advanced heart-failure planning.

papers.title: Sleep Deprivation, Occupational Stress, and Work-related Determinants of Sleep Disturbance Among Practicing Physicians: A Cross-sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation and occupational stress are increasingly recognized as critical determinants of physician well-being, with potential implications for healthcare quality and patient safety. However, data on sleep patterns and their determinants among heterogeneous groups of practicing physicians remain limited. To assess sleep patterns, lifestyle characteristics, and work-related stressors among practicing physicians and to examine their interrelationships. This cross-sectional, survey-based study was conducted between January and March 2026 among practicing physicians using an anonymous, self-administered electronic questionnaire. A total of 627 physicians participated. Data collected included demographic and professional characteristics, work patterns, lifestyle behaviors, sleep-related parameters, and perceived stress. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data. Among 627 physicians, 54.1% reported sleeping ≤6 h per night, and 51.9% experienced sleep disturbance at least twice per week. Nearly one-third (28.3%) reported working more than 60 h per week. Stress negatively affected sleep in 48.5% of respondents. The most common contributors to sleep disruption were anxiety or stress (44.2%) and patient emergencies (31.9%), while key work-related stressors included poor work-life balance (40.5%), administrative burden (36.5%), and high patient load (32.5%). Despite these findings, most physicians reported low tobacco and alcohol use and moderate levels of physical activity. Sleep deprivation and sleep disturbance are highly prevalent among practicing physicians and are strongly associated with work-related stressors rather than lifestyle factors. These findings highlight the need for system-level interventions targeting workload, scheduling, and workplace stress to improve physician sleep health and overall well-being.

papers.title: Neurogenic Tumors of the Larynx: Unusual Presentations in Two Case Studies.
papers.abstract: Benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors (BPNSTs) in the laryngeal and pharyngeal regions are rare; neurofibroma and schwannoma are two distinct histopathologic entities. The presence of these conditions in the laryngopharyngeal region may pose a diagnostic challenge because of their nonspecific clinical and endoscopic features. In this study, we report two cases of BPNSTs arising at unusual anatomical sites. The first case involved a 44-year-old man with a four-week history of dysphonia. Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy revealed bilateral edema and swelling of the true vocal folds, consistent with bilateral Reinke's edema, and subsequent direct laryngoscopy demonstrated polypoidal degeneration involving the anterior right true vocal fold. The lesion was excised, and histopathologic analysis with immunohistochemical staining confirmed the diagnosis of neurofibroma of the right vocal fold. The second case involved a 49-year-old woman who presented with a seven-month history of dysphagia, difficulty speaking, and sleep-disordered breathing. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a well-defined left oropharyngeal mass measuring approximately 2.1 × 2.5 × 2.0 cm. Direct laryngoscopy showed a firm, broad-based, smooth-edged mass arising from the left pharyngoepiglottic fold; complete excision was performed, and histopathologic examination confirmed schwannoma. These cases highlight the rare and diverse manifestations of BPNSTs in the laryngopharyngeal region. Neurofibroma and schwannoma should both be considered in the differential diagnosis of laryngeal and pharyngeal masses. Histopathologic examination remains essential for establishing the definitive diagnosis.

papers.title: Sleep Characteristics in Adolescents with Major Depressive Disorder: Associations with Non-Suicidal Self-Injury and Suicidality.
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep disturbances impact outcomes in major depressive disorder (MDD). This cross-sectional study evaluated subjective sleep quality and habits in adolescents with MDD and their associations with suicide attempt (SA) and non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI). Methods: Sixty-eight adolescents aged 13-18 years with MDD were classified as NSSI-only, SA-only, and combined. Clinical severity and depressive symptoms were measured with Clinical Global Impression-Severity scale and Children's Depression Rating Scale-Revised (CDRS-R). Self-harm and suicidality were evaluated using Inventory of Statements About Self-Injury and Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale. Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ) assessed past-month sleep quality and past-week sleep habits. Results: Participants had poor sleep quality (89.7%) and disturbed sleep habits (83.8%), without group differences. CSHQ scores correlated moderately with lifetime NSSI frequency (r = .36, P = .003), whereas PSQI scores correlated weakly (r = .28, P = .023). PSQI scores were modestly related to past-month suicidal ideation severity (r = .28, P = .022). In hierarchical regressions controlling for sedative medications and CDRS-R scores, CSHQ (β = 0.299, P = .022) and PSQI (β = 0.248, P = .047) accounted for incremental variance in lifetime NSSI frequency. Conclusion: Sleep problems are common among adolescents with MDD, suggesting a clinical feature rather than a subgroup-specific trait. Sleep disturbance was associated with lifetime NSSI burden beyond depression severity, indicating a clinically relevant assessment domain. Prospective longitudinal studies should clarify temporal and bidirectional relationships with self-harm outcomes.

papers.title: A Mixed-Precision CNN-LSTM Accelerator Featuring Long-Kernel Memory Reuse and Dynamic Quantization for Sleep Staging.
papers.abstract: This letter presents a mixed-precision CNN-LSTM accelerator for EEG-based sleep staging. To efficiently execute long temporal convolutions, a serpentine dataflow propagates activations between neighboring processing elements, reducing memory accesses by 6.2× and 2.25× compared with output- and weight-stationary dataflows, respectively. A hybrid quantization scheme applies runtime dynamic quantization to the LSTM and MLP layers and assigns mixed precision on a layer-by-layer basis, reducing model size by 4.16×. Combined with a bit-flexible MAC architecture and channel-grouped memory scheduling, the accelerator supports INT2/4/8/16 inference. Fabricated in 65 nm CMOS, the accelerator consumes 0.40 mW and achieves a 258× speedup over an iso-frequency 32b RISC-V processor. Evaluated across all 62 subjects in the public MASS-SS3 dataset using 31-fold leave-two-subject-out cross-validation, the mixed-precision approach with hybrid quantization maintains 5-class accuracy within 0.15% of the floating-point baseline when optimized for general sleep staging and N3 sensitivity within 0.51% when optimized for deep-sleep detection. The developed techniques are broadly applicable to EEG-based DL workloads.

papers.title: Interleukin-8 levels partially account for the indirect relationship between alcohol use disorder and global sleep quality in a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbance is common in alcohol use disorder (AUD). Inflammation may play a role in the relationship between alcohol use and sleep disturbance. Interleukin-8 (IL-8), a pro-inflammatory chemokine, may be implicated in this relationship. Therefore, this study investigated the role of IL-8 in the relationship between AUD and sleep disturbance. Sixty-two individuals with AUD (35 M/27 F) and 64 controls (33 M/31 F) completed the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), a self-report questionnaire assessing past-month sleep quality and disturbances, and provided blood samples to assess IL-8 levels. Univariate analyses of covariance (ANCOVAs) compared groups on PSQI global scores and IL-8 levels. An indirect cross-sectional association analysis tested if diagnostic group and PSQI global scores were indirectly associated via IL-8 levels. Individuals with AUD had higher PSQI global scores (F = 11.08, p = .001), indicating worse sleep, and higher IL-8 levels (F = 7.35, p = .008) compared to controls. AUD diagnosis was associated with higher IL-8 levels (a = 0.129, p = .008), and higher IL-8 levels were associated with worse PSQI scores (b = 3.157, p = .012). A partial indirect association effect was found where AUD diagnosis influenced PSQI scores through IL-8 levels (ab = 0.407, 95% CI = 0.062, 0.905); the direct effect of group on PSQI scores remained significant (c' = 1.864, p = .005). Results suggest that AUD diagnosis is associated with worse sleep, partially through an association with greater IL-8 levels. Identifying a role for IL-8 as a link between AUD and sleep disturbance will need to be tested in longitudinal studies. If replicated, IL-8 inhibition may offer a novel treatment target for those with AUD and comorbid sleep disorders. This article is part of the Sleep and Circadian Mechanisms in Mental Health Collection.

papers.title: Sleep and social behavior: neural interactions of sleep regulation and social dominance.
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders can perpetuate mental health conditions and negative social interactions. Additionally, research shows that individuals who develop socially debilitating disorders like PTSD, anxiety, and depression also report increased sleep disturbances. Exacerbating this issue, increased sleep debt due to sleep disruption from mental illness can potentiate further sleep dysregulation. Chronic social stress can lead to the development of sleep disorders, due to negative interactions in both natural and manmade power dynamics (including parent, employer, and even government related stressors). Hierarchical dynamics can lead to inequitable treatment and widespread health consequences, due to environmentally-imposed social dominance. At present, researchers are investigating behavioral and neural connections of sleep regulation and negative social interactions in mental health, including the impacts of these social dominance structures. For example, several limbic circuits, including the extended amygdala, hypothalamus, and medial prefrontal cortex have been identified in regulating sleep and social stress interactions. These neural connectivity patterns underlie mechanisms of how maladaptive responses to stress are associated with poor sleep regulation, providing novel targets for potential behavioral or neuromodulatory therapies. Our review explores discoveries regarding sleep and social behaviors in both human and rodent models, including current studies on neural mechanisms and genetic markers involved in the impacts of social stress-related dominance hierarchies on sleep/wake regulation. Establishing how social dynamics directly affect sleep quality and stress-related behaviors, and the reciprocal, will add to the growing body of research connecting disordered sleep to mental illness progression. This paper is part of the Sleep and Circadian Mechanisms in Mental Health Collection.

papers.title: Telemedicine for regional sleep patients-translating sleep services closer to home-TRENCH pilot study protocol.
papers.abstract: Poor sleep affects up to 45 percent of Australians and regional patients are further disadvantaged in accessing sleep services for diagnosis and management. This is particularly relevant in Queensland, where 36 percent of the state's population reside outside of metropolitan areas. This 12-month Hybrid Type I implementation pilot project will implement a telehealth-led, delivered and governed, local sleep service pathway encompassing screening, diagnosis, treatment, and on-going management for patients with suspected sleep disorders in Rockhampton. This major regional center has no existing public diagnostic and treatment sleep service; therefore service delivery will be managed and overseen by the existing Respiratory and Sleep Investigations Unit of the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital in Brisbane, Australia, located 637 km away. The aim of this study is to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and implementation success of a telehealth-led model of care that delivers sleep services closer to home for regional patients. The study adopts a Hybrid Type I effectiveness-implementation design, with implementation success assessed using the Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance framework. Primary outcomes will evaluate implementation success through assessment of patient and service reach, implementation fidelity, service adoption, stakeholder acceptability, and the potential sustainability of the model. Secondary outcomes will evaluate service and patient-level effectiveness, including successful completion of diagnostic testing, treatment initiation, reduction in travel requirements, and longer-term adherence to prescribed therapies. This model is designed to provide a sustainable sleep service that reduces patient barriers to receiving expert, tertiary level sleep care while affording improved service efficiency, cost-effective service delivery, optimal patient satisfaction, and improved health outcomes.
papers.journal: Sleep advances : a journal of the Sleep Research Society

papers.title: Circadian modulation of dopamine release shapes reward-evoked signaling in the nucleus accumbens.
papers.abstract: The circadian system is an important regulator of reward-related neural function and behavior. Dopamine (DA) release in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) is a key component of reward processing, yet how circadian timing shapes DA release in relation to reward behavior remains unclear. Here, we investigated circadian rhythms in DA release and reward behavior in C57BL/6J mice expressing the genetically encoded DA sensor DA3m in the NAc using long-term fiber photometry paired with an automated reward delivery and measurement system. Spontaneous DA, reflecting broad changes in DA release during natural behavior, peaked during the early subjective day. In a separate group of mice, targeted disruption of the molecular clock gene Bmal1 in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) strongly attenuated spontaneous DA rhythmicity, supporting a role for the SCN molecular clock in regulating these rhythms. Reward-evoked DA peaked during the day-to-night transition, while cue-evoked DA and reward behavior peaked during the early subjective night. Linear mixed-effects modeling showed that reward-evoked DA was positively associated with reward behavior and cue-evoked DA but negatively associated with baseline DA measured immediately before reward availability. Reward-evoked DA differed across circadian time even after accounting for reward behavior or cue-evoked DA, while higher baseline DA predicted smaller reward-evoked responses and the strength of this relationship also changed across circadian time. Together, these findings show that circadian time changes both the magnitude of reward-evoked DA responses and how those responses relate to baseline and cue-evoked dopamine signaling and reward behavior.

papers.title: Psychiatric Adverse Events Associated With Lebrikizumab: An FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) Disproportionality Analysis With an Indication-Matched Active Comparator.
papers.abstract: Lebrikizumab, an anti-interleukin-13 antibody approved for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, has not been evaluated for psychiatric adverse event reporting, although dupilumab and tralokinumab, which act on the same pathway, have generated postmarketing psychiatric signals, most consistently for sleep disturbance. We performed a disproportionality analysis of FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) reports accessed through the FDA Health Informatics initiative, openFDA (data through July 30, 2026), reported according to the READUS-PV (REporting of A Disproportionality analysis for drUg Safety signal detection using individual case safety reports in PharmacoVigilance) guideline. All exposure arms and the whole-database reference were restricted to reports received from September 2024, when lebrikizumab was approved in the United States, through June 2026. Reporting odds ratios (RORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) compared lebrikizumab with an indication-matched active comparator (dupilumab and tralokinumab) and, contextually, with the entire database, for a composite of psychiatric MedDRA (Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities) preferred terms from which any term showing a comparator-specific signal against the whole database was removed by a prespecified rule. The analysis included 1,743 lebrikizumab, 142,906 dupilumab, and 3,315 tralokinumab reports. Of 51 psychiatric terms identified, five were excluded for comparator-specific signals. For the 46-term composite, 38 lebrikizumab reports (2.2%) and 2,716 pooled comparator reports (1.9%) qualified; the ROR was 1.18 (95% CI, 0.85 to 1.63) against the pooled comparator, 1.17 (95% CI, 0.85 to 1.62) against dupilumab, 1.37 (95% CI, 0.90 to 2.09) against tralokinumab, and 0.42 (95% CI, 0.31 to 0.58) against the whole database. The full 51-term composite gave RORs of 0.44 to 0.77, the difference attributable to the excluded terms. A composite without sleep-wake terms gave 1.40 (95% CI, 0.94 to 2.06) against the pooled comparator and 2.08 (95% CI, 1.19 to 3.63) against tralokinumab. Nervousness and anxiety were nominally elevated against dupilumab and the pooled comparator; no term remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Within a common reporting period, psychiatric adverse events were not reported disproportionately for lebrikizumab relative to dupilumab or to the pooled indication-matched comparator. The higher estimates against tralokinumab alone rest on small numbers and warrant replication. These findings characterize reporting, not risk.
authors: João Marcelo Sá Pinto L de Oliveira

papers.title: Primary Care Physicians' Perspectives on Implementing Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia in Japan: A Qualitative Study Using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research.
papers.abstract: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is recommended as first-line treatment for chronic insomnia, but pharmacological treatment remains common. We explored primary care physicians' perspectives on implementing CBT-I in Japan. We conducted a qualitative descriptive study using a sequential inductive-deductive approach. Twenty-two primary care physicians from diverse regions and clinical settings participated in semi-structured interviews. Coding and theme development were conducted inductively following Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis, after which finalized themes were mapped onto the original Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. The analysis generated 53 analytic categories and five higher order themes: valuing collaborative non-pharmacological care; limitations of sleep hygiene education; limited confidence and competing priorities; need for simplified and standardized CBT-I; and need for professional and organizational support. Participants valued reducing reliance on medication but lacked confidence in explaining and delivering CBT-I, especially for patients with comorbidities. They requested brief explanations, flowcharts, patient-facing materials, training, feedback, and interprofessional support. Primary care physicians valued behavioral insomnia care but lacked a feasible pathway for routine delivery. Brief structured approaches, practical tools, and professional and organizational support may improve access to CBT-I in primary care.
papers.journal: Journal of general and family medicine

papers.title: The Growing Role of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Neuropsychiatry.
papers.abstract: The co-occurrence of metabolic and psychiatric disorders poses a major challenge in medicine, and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have emerged as candidates for neuropsychiatric repurposing given the wide distribution of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptors in brain regions governing mood, cognition, and reward. This narrative review summarizes central and peripheral mechanisms linking GLP-1 signaling to neuropsychiatric outcomes, critically appraises clinical evidence across psychiatric and neurodegenerative domains, and proposes a framework for integrating GLP-1RAs into neuropsychiatric care. A targeted search of PubMed/MEDLINE and ClinicalTrials.gov (January 2015-August 2026) prioritized randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, and prospective cohorts reporting neuropsychiatric outcomes. Four converging mechanisms- neuroinflammation, metabolic-vascular neuroprotection, synaptic plasticity, and mesolimbic reward modulation- underpin this rationale. The strongest and most clinically actionable evidence supports GLP-1RA use for antipsychotic-induced metabolic dysfunction, with trials in clozapine/olanzapine-treated patients showing substantial weight loss and glycemic normalization without psychiatric worsening or altered clozapine levels. By contrast, in Alzheimer's disease, despite consistent observational signals of 33-53% dementia risk reduction, Phase 3 EVOKE/EVOKE+ trials found no benefit of oral semaglutide in early symptomatic disease despite biomarker engagement, favoring a prevention- rather than treatment-focused framework. Evidence in Parkinson's disease and major depressive disorder remains more limited: motor benefit in Parkinson's disease appears restricted to short-acting agents, with the largest phase 3 trial negative, while broad antidepressant efficacy is unsupported, although semaglutide improved effort-based decision-making in anhedonic, metabolically burdened patients. Additional signals exist for alcohol use disorder, binge eating disorder, and obstructive sleep apnea. Psychiatric safety appears reassuring across meta-analyses of over 133,000 participants, though exclusion of psychiatric populations from pivotal trials limits generalizability. Current evidence supports selective, investigational use of GLP-1RAs in neuropsychiatric care- most robustly for antipsychotic-induced metabolic dysfunction- rather than generalized repurposing, pending adequately powered trials with neuropsychiatric endpoints, structured monitoring, and equitable access strategies.

papers.title: Isocaloric substitution of plant-based for animal-based protein and physical fitness in adolescents: a cross-sectional study from the EHDLA study.
papers.abstract: Plant and animal protein sources have been associated with health outcomes, but evidence on physical fitness within isocaloric substitution frameworks remains limited. This study examined whether modeled isocaloric substitutions between plant- and animal-derived protein sources were associated with physical fitness in adolescents. This cross-sectional analysis included adolescents aged 12-17 years from Spain. Source-specific protein variables were estimated from a 45-item food frequency questionnaire using reported consumption frequencies, standard portion sizes, and food-composition values. Physical fitness was evaluated using the Assessing the Levels of Physical Activity and Fitness (ALPHA-Fit). Using robust linear regression models, the association between a theoretical 5%-energy plant-for-animal protein contrast and physical fitness was estimated, while adjusting for age, sex, socioeconomic status, sleep duration, physical activity, sedentary behavior, body mass index, total energy intake, and energy from other macronutrients. The analytical sample comprised 790 adolescents (55.1% girls; median age: 14.0 years). Median energy intake was 2,585.9 kcal⋅day-1. No associations were observed between the modeled 5% of total-energy substitution of animal protein by plant protein and physical fitness outcomes (all p > 0.05). In food-level models, the theoretical substitution of egg-derived protein by plant protein was associated with lower standing long jump performance (standardized beta coefficient [β] = -0.55, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -1.06 to -0.06) and slower 4 × 10 m performance (β = 0.58, 95% CI: 0.12 to 1.04). A similar association with slower 4 × 10 m performance was observed for the modeled substitution of oily-fish-derived protein by plant protein (β = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.65). The theoretical substitution of root-vegetable-derived protein by animal protein was inversely associated with overall physical fitness (β = -1.23, 95% CI: -2.17 to -0.29), whereas the modeled substitution of cereal-derived protein by animal protein was associated with faster 4 × 10 m performance (β = -0.53, 95% CI: -0.89 to -0.17). In adolescents, modeled isocaloric substitutions between plant- and animal-derived protein sources were not associated with overall physical fitness, although food-level analyses showed heterogeneous associations, suggesting the relevance of the broader food matrix.

papers.title: Psychedelics and Sleep: Preclinical and Human Studies-A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Background: Classic psychedelics, including LSD, psilocybin, and N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT)/ayahuasca, have shown promise as rapid-acting treatments for psychiatric disorders. Because sleep plays a central role in emotional regulation and neuroplasticity, psychedelic-induced changes in sleep architecture are of interest. Methods: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed was searched for preclinical and clinical studies published up to May 1, 2026, investigating psychedelics and sleep-related outcomes. Twelve eligible studies evaluated LSD, psilocybin, or DMT/ayahuasca and assessed sleep architecture, sleep quality, electroencephalographic activity, or dreams. Study validity was assessed using appropriate methodological tools. Results: Preclinical studies consistently demonstrated acute REM sleep suppression, delayed REM onset, increased wakefulness, and transient disruption of non-REM sleep. Human findings were more heterogeneous, although randomized trials reported prolonged REM latency after psilocybin and reduced REM duration after ayahuasca. Evidence regarding slow-wave activity (SWA) was mixed, with ayahuasca increasing early-cycle SWA and psilocybin reducing absolute delta power during the first sleep cycle. Subjective sleep quality showed little acute change in controlled trials, whereas one large naturalistic study reported reductions in sleep disturbances following psilocybin. Administration close to bedtime appeared more disruptive than daytime dosing. In general, quality assessments indicated fair-to-poor validity and notable risk of bias. Conclusions: Classic psychedelics produce acute but transient alterations in sleep physiology, particularly affecting REM sleep. Whether these changes contribute to therapeutic effects remains uncertain. Larger, well-controlled studies using standardized polysomnographic methods are needed to clarify the relationship between psychedelic-induced sleep modulation and clinical outcomes. This review was not prospectively registered.

papers.title: Predictors of Anesthetic Augmentation in Electroconvulsive Therapy: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Background: Anesthetic augmentation with aminophylline and/or remifentanil is commonly used to prolong seizure duration when propofol-based electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) results in inadequate seizures. We aimed to identify independent predictors of subsequent augmentation use and develop an exploratory risk score. Methods: This retrospective cohort study (January-December 2015, single center) included 527 patients (4,016 ECT sessions) who received propofol anesthesia. Patients were categorized as propofol-only (n=357) or augmentation (n=170) group. Multiple logistic regression was used to identify predictors of augmentation. ANCOVA compared the effect of different adjunctive agents on post-adjunct seizure duration. Results: Shorter first-session electroencephalography (EEG) seizure duration (OR = 0.968, P < .001) and higher first-session seizure-inducing energy (OR = 1.044, P < .001) independently predicted augmentation, while age was not significant (P = .120). All three augmentation strategies significantly prolonged seizure duration; although, the sample sizes for individual agents (aminophylline n=85, remifentanil n=44, combination n=41) precluded a definitive comparative analysis; the ANCOVA revealed no significant differences between agents (F=0.967, P = .382). CGI scores were comparable between groups at baseline (P = .412) and discharge (P = .321). An exploratory risk score based on the two significant predictors showed good discriminative ability (AUC = 0.786). Conclusion: First-session EEG seizure duration and stimulation energy are practical predictors of subsequent augmentation use, whereas age is not independently predictive. No statistically significant difference in post-adjunct seizure duration was detected among the three adjunctive strategies and augmentation is associated with comparable clinical improvement. External validation of the proposed risk score is required before clinical implementation.

papers.title: Sleep Quality and Glycaemic Control in Adults with Type 2 Diabetes: Associations with Metabolic Parameters, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and Appetite-Regulating Hormones.
papers.abstract: To determine prevalence of poor sleep quality using Pittsburgh University Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and its association with glycaemic control, dyslipidaemia, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), leptin, and ghrelin in type 2 diabetes (T2DM). This cross-sectional study enrolled 216 adults with T2DM from a tertiary care hospital in North India. Sleep quality was assessed using PSQI. Fasting blood samples were analysed for HbA1c, glucose, lipids, insulin, leptin, and acylated ghrelin. NAFLD was assessed by ultrasound. Correlation between sleep quality and different metabolic parameters was assessed. Poor sleep quality (PSQI > 5) was present in 39.8% of participants. The global PSQI score correlated significantly with higher HbA1c (r = 0.173, P = 0.011) and fasting plasma glucose (FPG) (r = 0.223, P = 0.001). Among the PSQI components, sleep latency and sleep disturbances (components 4 and 5) had most significant associations with poorer glycaemic control (P < 0.050). In regression models, a bidirectional relationship was observed: Higher fasting plasma glucose independently predicted worse PSQI scores (β = 0.27, P = 0.023), and worse PSQI scores independently predicted higher fasting plasma glucose (β = 4.20, P = 0.006). Poorer sleep also correlated with higher total and LDL cholesterol (P < 0.050). No significant associations were found between sleep quality and NAFLD, serum leptin, or ghrelin. There was a high prevalence of poor sleep quality in Indian patients with T2DM. Regression analysis revealed a bidirectional link between poor sleep and poor glycaemic control. This suggests that poor sleep quality correlates with glycaemic and metabolic dysregulation, hence highlighting sleep as a critical, modifiable target for diabetes management.
papers.journal: Indian journal of endocrinology and metabolism

papers.title: Exploring unknown subgroups in sleep disturbance: a mixture regression approach for college students pre- and during COVID-19 in Hawaii.
papers.abstract: College students have a high propensity for disordered sleep. Combined with disruptions due to the COVID-19 pandemic, there may be an increased tendency for disordered sleep patterns. The current study focuses on both identification of subgroups of disordered sleep college students before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as determining demographic differences between the groups. This study used mixture regression model analysis (MRM) to evaluate the effects of age; gender; Body Mass Index; Grade Point Average; and lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer or questioning identification on sleep disturbance scores. Two independent samples from a university in Hawaii, collected before (n = 216) and during the COVID-19 pandemic (n = 177), were analyzed to explore the heterogenous patterns of sleep quality and related factors, addressing inconsistent findings on the pandemic's impact. The MRM revealed two latent groups within Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores across datasets from 2020 and 2021: "typical college sleepers" and "disordered college sleepers." Before the pandemic, typical sleepers had an average PSQI score of 4.89, while disordered sleepers averaged 8.36. During the pandemic, heterogeneity persisted: typical sleepers scored 6.81, while disordered sleepers averaged 14.38. Demographic and academic factors influenced the two groups differently. The MRM effectively identified latent groups with different sleep disturbance scores, offering insights into previously undetected differential relationships between students' characteristics, risk factors, and sleep outcomes. Furthermore, our study demonstrated that MRMs are a suitable tool for addressing heterogeneity in sleep quality research.
papers.journal: Sleep advances : a journal of the Sleep Research Society

papers.title: Comparing 6-sulfatoxymelatonin collected from liquid and dried urine samples: a proof-of-concept study.
