papers.title: Sample size critically shapes the reliability of EEG case-control findings in psychiatry.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) studies in psychiatry have produced highly inconsistent findings, particularly in case-control designs. Small sample sizes are widely assumed to contribute to this variability, yet their impact on the reliability of EEG group comparisons has not been systematically quantified at scale. Here, we address this key gap using a large multisite resting-state EEG dataset comprising 2,874 participants aged 5-18 years, including individuals with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, anxiety, learning disorders, and healthy controls. We extracted a comprehensive set of spectral, temporal, and complexity EEG features and performed repeated case-control comparisons across a wide range of sample sizes using extensive random subsampling. Results from small samples were unstable, with inflated and highly variable effect sizes across iterations. In contrast, larger samples produced consistent and reproducible findings, converging on uniformly small but robust effects. Statistical power rose steeply with sample size, whereas false positive rates remained relatively stable. These results demonstrate the central role of sample size in shaping EEG study outcomes and challenge the utility of conventional case-control approaches for biomarker discovery in psychiatry.

papers.title: Effects of Agomelatine on Sleep Quality, Anxiety, Depression, Appetite, and Fatigue During Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation: A Triple-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Trial.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances, anxiety, depression, reduced appetite, and fatigue are common among patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and can adversely affect quality of life and recovery. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of agomelatine on sleep quality, anxiety, depression, appetite, and fatigue in patients undergoing HSCT. In this clinical trial, 165 candidates were screened, and 90 patients undergoing HSCT were randomly assigned using block randomization to receive agomelatine 25 mg nightly or a matching placebo throughout hospitalization, which lasted approximately 1 month. Outcomes were assessed at admission, during the neutropenic phase, and at discharge using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, Brief Fatigue Inventory, and Council on Nutrition Appetite Questionnaire. Analyses were performed using STATA version 17, with a significance threshold of P < 0.05. Crude group comparisons showed favorable trends in global PSQI score and its components, anxiety, depression, and appetite with agomelatine relative to placebo; most differences were not statistically significant. Fatigue showed no significant overall between-group benefit, although scores changed over time. Group-by-time interactions were statistically significant. Mean changes in PSQI component scores were lower with agomelatine across the 3 assessment periods. In particular, the mean change in the PSQI sleep-medication component score was approximately 0.5 units lower with agomelatine than with placebo (β = -0.49; 95% CI, -0.90 to -0.09; P = 0.016). No statistically significant between-group difference in reported adverse events was observed. Agomelatine may have a supportive role during HSCT, particularly in relation to a lower PSQI sleep-medication component score. The negative crude coefficient for the global PSQI score also favored agomelatine, although this comparison was not statistically significant. Reported adverse events did not differ significantly between groups. Larger trials, including trials evaluating a higher dose, are required to confirm treatment effects on sleep and psychological outcomes.
papers.journal: Iranian journal of pharmaceutical research : IJPR

papers.title: Multimodal versus Conventional Opioid-Based Analgesia and Postoperative Outcomes After Breast Cancer Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: To compare the effects of a structured multimodal analgesia (MMA) protocol versus conventional opioid-based analgesia (OBA) on postoperative pain, chronic postsurgical pain (CPSP), sleep quality, opioid consumption, and recovery outcomes after breast cancer surgery. This retrospective cohort study included 260 female patients who underwent breast cancer surgery between June 2022 and May 2024. Patients were divided into an OBA group (n = 142) and an MMA group (n = 118) according to perioperative analgesic strategy. The OBA group received morphine patient-controlled intravenous analgesia (PCIA) plus oral acetaminophen/ibuprofen; the MMA group additionally received preoperative gabapentin, intraoperative-to-postoperative dexmedetomidine infusion, and wound local anesthetic infiltration. Acute postoperative pain was evaluated using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) at 1, 6, 12, and 24 hours after surgery. CPSP incidence was assessed at 3 and 6 months postoperatively. Sleep quality was measured using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), while postoperative recovery was assessed using the QoR-15 questionnaire. Opioid consumption and opioid-related adverse effects during the first 48 postoperative hours were also compared. Patients in the MMA group had significantly lower VAS scores at all postoperative time points compared with the OBA group (mean differences 0.23-0.37 points on a 0-10 scale; all P<0.01). CPSP incidence was lower in the MMA group at 3 months (22.9% vs 39.4%; odds ratio [OR] 2.19, 95% CI 1.27-3.79, favoring OBA-to-MMA risk) and at 6 months (15.3% vs 28.2%; OR 2.18, 95% CI 1.17-4.05). MMA was also associated with lower postoperative opioid consumption (mean differences 1.9-2.7 mg over 0-48 hours), fewer opioid-related adverse effects (nausea, vomiting, and sedation; ORs 2.3-2.6, all 95% CI excluding 1), better PSQI sleep-quality scores (mean differences 0.55-0.61 points), and higher QoR-15 recovery scores (mean differences 2.6-3.5 points) compared with OBA (all P<0.05). In this retrospective cohort, a structured MMA protocol was associated with lower acute postoperative pain scores, a lower incidence of chronic postsurgical pain, better sleep quality, lower opioid consumption, and better recovery scores after breast cancer surgery compared with routine opioid-based analgesia. As an observational, non-randomized comparison, these findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating; prospective randomized trials are needed to confirm a causal benefit before firm practice recommendations can be made.

papers.title: Tracing memory suppression and transformation: interplay of cognitive, neural, and cultural dynamics.
papers.abstract: Episodic memory plays a fundamental role in shaping cognition, identity, and decision making, yet it is not a fixed record of past experiences and can be actively modified through various cognitive processes. What people remember about their own lives, and what they report to others, is shaped by processes that weaken, block, or displace competing traces. This narrative review integrates three related but distinct forms of forgetting: denial induced forgetting (DIF), retrieval induced forgetting (RIF), and suppression induced forgetting (SIF). For each, we summarize the behavioral evidence, the available neurophysiological markers, and the implications for criminological, clinical, and cultural questions. DIF, a comparatively recent phenomenon, shows that repeatedly denying details of an experienced event can undermine later memory for the interview in which the denial occurred, and sometimes for the event itself, yet it currently lacks direct neurophysiological evidence. RIF and SIF are better characterized in terms of neuro-electrophysiological activity, with converging work on prefrontal control, theta and alpha/beta oscillations, and hippocampal down-regulation. We propose that the three phenomena can be conceptualized along a continuum from incidental to intentional memory control, while recognizing that their underlying mechanisms may differ. Their forensic relevance lies in how testimony is elicited and evaluated, and cultural norms may shape when, how, and why people deny, selectively retrieve, or suppress memories. We close by identifying gaps in ecological validity, neural evidence for DIF, the separation of voluntary and involuntary control, and cross-cultural work, and by proposing multimodal, interdisciplinary research to address them.

papers.title: The regenerative hexagon: six domains shaping musculoskeletal regenerative outcomes.
papers.abstract: The classical regenerative triad of scaffold, cells, and growth factors has guided musculoskeletal regenerative medicine for over two decades, yet outcome variability after orthobiologic treatment is not explained by preparation parameters alone. Contemporary regenerative biology already recognizes that host immunity, mechanics, and metabolism shape repair; what is less developed is a framework that integrates these dimensions for orthobiologic treatment and states their interactions in testable form. We propose an update of the triad concept rather than a replacement of it: a Regenerative Hexagon that retains the three construct components and adds three host-state domains that modify the response to them. These are the Systemic Host Environment, encompassing the gut-joint axis, sleep, medications, conditioning, metabolic status, and the pre-existing immune profile; Biomechanics and Mechanotransduction; and Cellular Energetics, defined as the energetic and redox state of resident and administered cells, which biophysical modalities are proposed to modify. Six short diagonals connect non-adjacent vertices, forming two interlocking triads that generate the Regenerative Star, and the framework is read as a sequence of states across the phases of repair rather than as a static configuration. The evidence for each component is graded with explicit criteria, and interactions demonstrated within a single experimental system are separated from those inferred from separate literatures. Convergent mechanisms are proposed: sleep fragmentation in healthy volunteers and dysbiosis-derived endotoxin in mechanistic studies both engage Toll-like receptor 4 signalling, and host metabolic burden was associated with orthobiologic response in a preparation-dependent manner. We hypothesize that the pillars interact multiplicatively rather than additively, a proposition not yet supported by a quantitative model and testable in factorial trials. The Regenerative Star is offered as a hypothesis-generating framework rather than a validated clinical instrument, reorienting inquiry from which preparation is superior toward in which host a given preparation performs.

papers.title: Magnetomyography for skeletal muscle function assessment: prospective applications in sarcopenia.
papers.abstract: Sarcopenia is a progressive and generalized skeletal muscle disorder characterized by loss of muscle strength, reduced muscle quantity or quality, and impaired physical performance. It is associated with adverse outcomes including falls, fractures, physical disability, and mortality, and represents a growing global health concern. However, currently available clinical assessments provide limited information on the electrophysiological and neuromuscular alterations that may precede overt functional decline. Magnetomyography (MMG)-here defined as the non-invasive detection of biomagnetic fields generated by skeletal muscle electrical activity and distinguished from mechanomyography-offers a contactless approach to characterizing muscle electrophysiology. Recent advances in optically pumped magnetometers, portable magnetic shielding, and signal-processing methods have expanded the feasibility of MMG for detecting muscle action potentials, motor-unit activity, fatigue-related changes, and training adaptations. In this perspective review, we summarize the principles and technological development of MMG, critically evaluate current evidence for skeletal muscle assessment, and discuss its potential relevance to sarcopenia. In particular, we propose a conceptual framework in which MMG could complement established assessments by characterizing neuromuscular integrity, investigating potential neural and muscular contributions to functional decline, and monitoring responses to intervention. Importantly, direct evidence in individuals with sarcopenia is currently lacking, and MMG remains an experimental rather than clinically validated diagnostic approach.

papers.title: Associations Between Weight Loss and Actigraphy-Assessed Sleep Health Indicators in Adults Following Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery.
papers.abstract: While metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) leads to substantial weight loss, objective multidimensional assessments of sleep health in free-living adults after surgery are limited. This study examined associations between weight loss and actigraphy-assessed sleep health indicators among adults undergoing MBS. Data were pooled from two prospective cohort studies including 100 adults scheduled for sleeve gastrectomy or Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Participants wore wrist-worn accelerometers for 7-10 days at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months post-surgery. Five sleep health indicators, including sleep regularity, wake-up time variability, sleep duration, sleep efficiency, and sleep timing, were derived using GGIR. Percent total weight loss (%TWL) was calculated at each follow-up. Linear mixed models assessed changes over time and associations between sleep changes and %TWL, adjusting for wear time and relevant covariates. Mean %TWL was 22.1 ± 6.2% at 6 months and 24.8 ± 8.8% at 12 months. No significant group-level changes in sleep indicators were observed (all p ≥ 0.20). However, greater %TWL was associated with better sleep regularity, reflected by higher Sleep Regularity Index scores (B = 0.349, p = 0.02) and lower wake-up time variability (B = -0.044, p = 0.04). Sleep duration, efficiency, and timing were not significantly associated with %TWL. At baseline, sleep duration (8.2 h/day), efficiency (86.8%), and midpoint (2:53 a.m.) were within recommended ranges, whereas Sleep Regularity Index scores were low (33.5), indicating substantial day-to-day variability in sleep timing. MBS did not improve overall sleep health, but greater postoperative weight loss was linked to better sleep regularity.

papers.title: Routine greenery encounters and anxiety occurrence probability: a study of component contributions in university residential greenery scenes based on mobile electroencephalography data.
papers.abstract: University students frequently encounter campus greenery during walking, queueing, and brief stops. Although green-space exposure has been associated with psychological restoration, the relationships between individual micro-scale greenery components and short-timescale anxiety-related electroencephalographic (EEG) responses remain unclear. This exploratory study examined associations between mobile EEG-derived Anxiety Occurrence Probability (AOP) and greenery components along an everyday campus route. A residential greenery site at a university in Nanjing, China, was studied during summer. Thirteen greenery components were quantified along a fixed 45-m walking and queueing route. Mobile EEG data were collected from 38 university students, of whom 35 with valid data were included in the final analysis. AOP was derived from frontal alpha asymmetry and theta/beta ratio relative to individual resting baselines. 82 scene measurement points were established. Spatial mapping combined isovist-based visual fields and inverse distance weighting. Associations between greenery components and AOP were examined using correlation, multiple linear regression, ridge regression, and piecewise linear regression. AOP showed substantial spatial heterogeneity across the route. Color richness, shading rate, green view ratio, and visibility were negatively associated with AOP (p < 0.05), whereas structural components showed no robust associations after accounting for multicollinearity. The regression model explained 79.8% of the variance in AOP (adjusted R 2 = 0.770; Cohen's f 2 = 3.957). Piecewise regression identified breakpoints of 0.321 for shading rate and 0.451 for visibility, with bootstrap 95% CIs of 0.28-0.36 and 0.40-0.50, respectively. Routine, low-intensity encounters with several visual-spatial greenery components were associated with lower AOP in this sample. Given the single-campus, single-season, fixed-route observational design and absence of a non-green control route, these findings are correlational and do not establish causality. The estimated breakpoints should be considered context-specific reference values requiring validation in larger, multi-site and multi-season studies.

papers.title: Adaptation needs of patients with obstructive sleep apnea during positive airway pressure therapy: a longitudinal qualitative study based on transition theory.
papers.abstract: This qualitative study aimed to explore the evolution of adaptation needs among patients with moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) during the initial phase of positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy, guided by Transition Theory, to provide references for improving patients' treatment adherence. The study employed a longitudinal qualitative design, adopting Transition Theory as the analytical framework. Data were collected through three rounds of semi-structured interviews with 12 moderate-to-severe OSA participants newly starting PAP therapy, recruited from the Sleep Medicine Department of a tertiary hospital in Shandong from March to July 2026. The interview material was analyzed using Colaizzi's seven-step analytical approach. Three core themes and nine sub-themes were extracted. (1) Initial Transition Period (1 week of treatment): Dual needs for physical safety and cognitive guidance. (2) Adjustment Period (1 month of treatment): Needs to resolve practical conflicts and sustain treatment motivation. (3) Stabilization Period (3 months of treatment): Needs for treatment acceptance and role transformation. This study shows that participants with OSA have a staged, dynamic adaptation process to PAP initial phase of therapy, supporting the applicability of Transition Theory in chronic disease management. Guided by this theory, healthcare professionals should provide phased continuous interventions matching participants' core needs at each stage, so as to help patients get through the initial treatment period smoothly and optimize health outcomes.

papers.title: Sleep quality and physical fitness among Chinese adolescents: a multilevel cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Sleep quality is an important component of adolescent health, but its association with physical fitness remains insufficiently understood. This study examined the association between sleep quality and physical fitness among Chinese adolescents. This school-based cross-sectional study included 5,018 adolescents from 18 schools in six Chinese cities. Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). The Physical Fitness Index (PFI) was the primary outcome, and estimated VO₂max was the secondary outcome. School-level random-intercept models adjusted for age, sex, school stage, BMI, socioeconomic status, and screen time. Sensitivity analyses examined school-clustered standard errors and exploratory models incorporating random intercepts for school and class within school. Higher PSQI scores were associated with modestly lower PFI in the fully adjusted school-only model (β = -0.049, 95% CI: -0.079 to -0.019, P = 0.002). The PFI association remained significant with school-clustered standard errors (95% CI: -0.086 to -0.012, P = 0.013) and in the exploratory school-and-class model (β = -0.040, 95% CI: -0.068 to -0.012, P = 0.005). For estimated VO₂max, the association was non-significant in the fully adjusted school-only model (β = -0.036, 95% CI: -0.082-0.010, P = 0.125), but significant in the exploratory school-and-class model (β = -0.049, 95% CI: -0.092 to -0.005, P = 0.030), indicating sensitivity to the clustering specification. Poorer sleep quality was modestly associated with lower PFI among Chinese adolescents. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to clarify temporal relationships and evaluate potential implications for health monitoring and fitness promotion.

papers.title: MVCNN model for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea prediction via facial photos.
papers.abstract: Polysomnography (PSG) is the gold standard for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) diagnosis but is limited for large-scale screening and telemedicine by high costs and specialized requirements. Given the close correlation between craniofacial features and OSA, this study developed a non-invasive risk stratification model (non-OSA, mild OSA, and moderate-to-severe OSA) using two-dimensional multi-view facial photographs based on a Multi-View Convolutional Neural Network (MVCNN). This multicenter retrospective study included 212 children with frontal and lateral facial photographs linked to polysomnography. Models were evaluated at the patient level after aggregating each participant's available image records. The MVCNN was internally evaluated in 149 patients and externally evaluated in 63 patients. Patient-level discrimination and classification metrics were estimated with bootstrap confidence intervals, and paired bootstrap analysis compared models evaluated on common patients. In the internal patient-level evaluation, MVCNN achieved a macro-AUC of 0.898 (95% CI, 0.863-0.930), macro-F1 of 0.839, balanced accuracy of 0.840, and overall accuracy of 0.846. Its macro-AUC exceeded those of ResNet-50 by 0.061 (95% CI, 0.022-0.106; P = 0.004) and VGG-16 by 0.104 (95% CI, 0.057-0.164; P < 0.001). In the external cohort, MVCNN achieved a macro-AUC of 0.876 (95% CI, 0.827-0.919), macro-F1 of 0.833, balanced accuracy of 0.826, and overall accuracy of 0.841. Patient-level analyses support the discriminatory performance of multi-view facial photography for pediatric OSA risk stratification in the studied dental cohorts. Prospective validation, direct view-ablation studies, and calibration in broader clinical populations are required before clinical deployment.

papers.title: Living under a "seismic time bomb": hyperarousal and insomnia severity in the context of anticipated earthquake threat.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are well documented following large-scale disasters; however, less is known about insomnia severity among individuals living with anticipated seismic threat before a major earthquake occurs. This study examined the associations among trauma-related symptom dimensions, emotional distress, and insomnia severity in a non-clinical sample of adults residing in Istanbul who had not experienced severe personal loss or major housing destruction due to a major earthquake. A total of 416 adults residing in Istanbul completed an online survey assessing depression, anxiety, stress, trauma-related symptom dimensions (intrusion, avoidance, and hyperarousal), and insomnia severity. Correlational analyses revealed positive associations among psychological distress, trauma-related symptom dimensions, and insomnia severity. No significant differences in insomnia severity were found across gender or age groups. In a simultaneous regression model, hyperarousal showed the strongest unique statistical association with insomnia severity (β = 0.716, p < 0.001). A sensitivity analysis excluding the sleep-related IES-R Item 15 attenuated this association, with intrusion becoming the strongest predictor in the modified model. Exploratory mediation analyses showed no statistically significant indirect effects through depression, anxiety, or stress. These findings suggest that hyperarousal was particularly strongly associated with insomnia severity within this sample living under anticipated earthquake threat. However, the cross-sectional design and overlap between IES-R hyperarousal and sleep-related content limit causal and construct-level interpretations.

papers.title: Changes in negative affect and resting-state EEG power following an EEG-derived generative reality art experience: a pilot pre-post study.
papers.abstract: Physiological signals are increasingly incorporated into personalized immersive media, but little is known about affective and neurophysiological changes when such signals are used as artistic material. This exploratory pilot study examined an electroencephalography (EEG)-derived generative virtual reality (VR) art experience in which participant-specific EEG signals were symbolically transformed into prompts for immersive visual environments. Thirty healthy university students completed the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule and resting-state EEG recordings before and after a single 5-min experience. EEG analyses examined log-transformed absolute alpha- and beta-band power across frontal, frontocentral, and central regions, with false discovery rate correction. Negative affect decreased from pre- to post-experience (mean change = -3.13, FDR-adjusted p = 0.004), whereas positive affect did not change significantly. Absolute beta-band power decreased across all three regions, and absolute alpha-band power decreased in the frontocentral and central regions (FDR-adjusted p values ≤0.022). Exploratory relative-power analyses showed no significant pre-post differences after correction for multiple comparisons. Frontal alpha asymmetry did not change significantly. Changes in EEG measures were not significantly associated with changes in affect after correction for multiple comparisons. The EEG findings therefore do not establish a neural mechanism for the reduction in negative affect. These findings indicate that the experience was associated with short-term changes in negative affect and resting-state spectral power. Because this pilot study used a single-group design, the findings do not establish causality or therapeutic efficacy. Instead, they provide an initial empirical basis for controlled research on physiological data as personalized material for immersive art and affective experience.

papers.title: Editorial: BCIs for monitoring and treating mental health conditions.
Problematic social media use and academic attainment in physical education undergraduates: conditional indirect associations through sleep, engagement, and persistence.
papers.abstract: Problematic social media use (PSMU) has been associated with poorer academic functioning, but the pathways linking dysregulated use with university attainment remain incompletely specified. This cross-sectional study tested whether sleep adequacy, classroom engagement, and academic persistence statistically mediated the association between PSMU and cumulative GPA, and whether bedtime social media use moderated the first of these pathways. Data from 800 Physical Education undergraduates at four university sites were analyzed using structural equation modelling and 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap samples. Participants had a mean age of 20.55 years (SD = 1.18); 62.6% identified as men, 35.4% as women, and 2.0% selected another gender category or preferred not to answer. Measures included the nine-item Social Media Disorder Scale for PSMU, behavioral and emotional engagement subscales from the Engagement versus Disaffection with Learning framework, the Intent-to-Persist component of the College Persistence Questionnaire, a sleep-adequacy composite of school-night sleep duration and perceived sleep quality, and a bedtime social media use timing-frequency item. Greater problematic use was associated with poorer sleep adequacy, which was linked to weaker engagement, lower persistence, and lower GPA. The full sequential indirect effect was significant. Bedtime social media use strengthened the negative association between problematic use and sleep adequacy and yielded significant moderated mediation. Findings were robust across alternative sleep indicators and GPA sources. Sleep, engagement, and persistence therefore represent statistically supported intermediate associations within the proposed model, although longitudinal research is needed to establish temporal ordering and reciprocal effects.

papers.title: 24-h movement behavior composition associated with mental health in preschool children: a cross-sectional compositional data analysis.
papers.abstract: Mental health problems in preschool children represent an important public health concern. Understanding the associations between 24-h movement behaviors, including moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), light physical activity (LPA), sedentary behavior (SB), and sleep (SLP), and mental health may help identify activity compositions associated with more favorable psychological outcomes. This study aimed to examine the associations between reallocations of time among 24-h movement behaviors and mental health in preschool children aged 3-6 years and to identify activity compositions associated with more favorable mental health outcomes. This cross-sectional study included 850 Chinese preschool children aged 3-6 years. MVPA, LPA, and SB were objectively measured using ActiGraph GT3X-BT accelerometers, whereas SLP was assessed using structured parent- and teacher-reported questionnaires. Mental health outcomes, including total difficulties, internalizing and externalizing problems, and prosocial behavior, were assessed using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). Compositional data analysis (CoDA) was performed using isometric log-ratio (ilr) transformations and multiple linear regression models. A one-to-three proportional time-reallocation approach was used to estimate changes in mental health outcomes associated with reallocating 10% of time in one behavior proportionally across the remaining three behaviors. In addition, optimal time-use analysis was conducted to identify 24-h movement compositions associated with more favorable mental health outcomes. Models were adjusted for age, gender, body mass index, residential district, parental education, and parental attitudes toward physical activity. An increase in MVPA was significantly associated with a reduction in Total Difficulties (β = -1.658, p < 0.001) and Internalizing Problems (β = -0.636, p = 0.027). An increase in SB was associated with an increase in Total Difficulties (β = 1.615, p = 0.032), while an increase in SLP was significantly associated with a reduction in Total Difficulties (β = -1.134, p = 0.034) and an improvement in Externalizing Problems (β = -1.642, p = 0.009). Increases in MVPA or SLP, when proportionally replacing the other three behaviors, as well as the substitution of SB with other behaviors, were all associated with improvements in mental health (p < 0.05). The model-derived 24-h movement behavior composition associated with more favorable mental health profiles in the study sample comprised 71 min of MVPA (55-85 min), 234 min of LPA (190-265 min), 514 min of SB (450-590 min), and 621 min of sleep (515-690 min). Greater relative time spent in MVPA and SLP was associated with more favorable mental health outcomes among preschool children. The model-derived 24-h movement behavior composition identified in this study reflects associations within the observed sample and should not be interpreted as a causal relationship or a prescriptive intervention target. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to validate these findings.

papers.title: Effects of cognitive behavioral therapy on psychological and physical outcomes in adults with rheumatoid arthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
papers.abstract: Pain and functional limitations associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) can substantially impair patients' psychological and physical well-being. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) may alleviate psychological and physical symptoms in patients with RA by modifying maladaptive cognitions and behaviors and promoting adaptive coping with the disease. However, the effect of CBT in RA patients has not been systematically established. PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Embase, and Web of Science were systematically searched from database inception to July 9, 2026, for relevant studies. Study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment were independently performed by two reviewers. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or adjudicated by a third reviewer. Meta-analyses were primarily implemented through random-effects models. Effect estimates were presented as standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Twelve RCTs involving 1,538 participants with RA were incorporated. CBT was associated with lower levels of depression (SMD = -0.35, 95% CI: -0.55 to -0.14, low-certainty evidence), anxiety (SMD = -0.20, 95% CI: -0.32 to -0.08, moderate-certainty evidence), and fatigue (SMD = -0.44, 95% CI: -0.66 to -0.22, low-certainty evidence). At the 6-month follow-up, the pooled SMDs were -0.42 (95% CI, -0.63 to -0.20) for depression and -0.22 (95% CI, -0.43 to -0.01) for anxiety, based on six RCTs with available follow-up data. For sleep, the pooled estimate favored CBT, although this finding was based on only two studies and was supported by very-low-certainty evidence. No statistically significant between-group differences were noted for pain, physical function, or quality-of-life (QoL). Substantial heterogeneity was observed for depression and fatigue, and the 95% prediction intervals crossed the line of no effect for both outcomes. Exploratory subgroup analyses by CBT delivery format revealed no significant differences between subgroups. The pooled estimates suggested that CBT may be associated with lower levels of fatigue, anxiety, and depression in patients with RA. However, substantial heterogeneity, prediction intervals crossing the line of no effect, and low certainty of evidence limit the reliability of these outcomes. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261470674, CRD420261470674.

papers.title: The human body as a multi-organ coupled homeostatic organism: the core mechanism of the super minimally invasive surgery paradigm.
papers.abstract: Super minimally invasive surgery (SMIS) has been proposed as a treatment paradigm in which minimally invasive care is evaluated not only by access-related trauma but also by treatment-induced biological disturbance and preservation of organ function. We hypothesize that, when disease-control adequacy is comparable, strategies associated with lower multidimensional homeostatic disturbance will be associated with faster functional recovery and better long-term organ- and patient-centered outcomes. We define an SMIS-concordant strategy by three conditions: adequate disease control; lower measurable treatment-induced disturbance than an appropriate comparator; and preservation or faster restoration of organ and systemic function. Homeostatic disturbance is operationalized as a multidomain construct that may include inflammatory/immune, neuroendocrine, metabolic/nutritional, organ-specific, barrier/microbiome/circadian, functional, and patient-reported domains. Because no validated universal score, weighting scheme, or threshold is available, we propose a comparative measurement matrix rather than a new composite index. The framework yields three falsifiable predictions: SMIS-concordant strategies should produce less early biological disturbance, support a faster return toward baseline, and provide prognostic information for long-term recovery beyond conventional perioperative measures. Early gastric cancer illustrates the approach: in guideline-eligible patients, endoscopic resection preserves the stomach and is associated with lower procedural burden and better quality of life, while preliminary proteomic data suggest less postoperative immune-inflammatory perturbation; gastrectomy remains indicated when curative criteria are not met. SMIS is therefore presented as an integrative treatment-decision framework that requires prospective validation.

papers.title: Associations of gastrointestinal, sleep, and affective symptom combinations with cardiometabolic conditions: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Gastrointestinal, sleep, and affective symptoms frequently co-occur, but their combined associations with cardiometabolic conditions are poorly characterized. We examined associations of specific symptom combinations and the number of co-occurring symptom domains with prevalent cardiometabolic conditions. This cross-sectional study included 5,203 adults aged ≥20 years from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2009-2010. Gastrointestinal, sleep, and affective symptoms were classified into eight mutually exclusive combinations. Survey-weighted logistic regression was used to examine associations with hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, adjusting for demographic characteristics, body mass index (BMI), and lifestyle factors. We also examined the number of co-occurring symptom domains (0-3) and performed sensitivity analyses using alternative symptom definitions. Compared with participants classified as negative for all three symptom domains, those with gastrointestinal and sleep symptoms (G+S) had higher adjusted odds of hypertension (odds ratio [OR], 1.92; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.27-2.89), as did those with all three domains (G+S+A; OR, 2.31; 95% CI, 1.38-3.86). Sleep and affective symptoms (S+A) were associated with dyslipidemia (OR, 1.67; 95% CI, 1.06-2.61), and G+S+A was associated with diabetes (OR, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.15-2.30). Increasing numbers of symptom domains showed positive trends for hypertension (P for trend = 0.007) and diabetes (P for trend = 0.041). No symptom combination showed a statistically significant adjusted association with metabolic syndrome. Associations of G+S+A with hypertension and diabetes were generally consistent across sensitivity analyses. Specific combinations of gastrointestinal, sleep, and affective symptoms were associated with prevalent cardiometabolic conditions, particularly hypertension and diabetes. Both symptom composition and the number of co-occurring domains warrant evaluation in longitudinal studies.

papers.title: A multimodal approach to identify atypical face processing in first episode psychosis (early schizophrenia spectrum disorders).
papers.abstract: While social interaction difficulties are common in schizophrenia, the neural underpinnings for its social symptomatology are under-explored. In this study, we aimed to isolate atypical neural systems associated with live social interaction in first episode psychosis (early schizophrenia spectrum disorder). A two-person live face gaze paradigm was employed as the behavioral proxy for social interaction while electroencephalography (EEG), functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), eye tracking, and facial movement measures were simultaneously acquired. Findings were compared for 24 first episode psychosis (FEP) patients and 32 typically developed (TD) participants to test the hypothesis that these neural and behavioral measures would isolate atypical social neural systems in the FEP group. FNIRS neural data showed atypical hemodynamic activity in the right temporoparietal region, known to be associated with live face-to-face interactions. This atypical activity was significantly correlated with expressive deficit score, a sub score derived from PANSS negative symptom domain and N4, a PANSS negative symptom which measures passive/apathetic social withdrawal. Involuntary behavioral responses associated with spontaneous facial mimicry and gaze fixation were reduced in FEP. Consistent with previous findings, Event Related Potential (ERP) amplitudes and latencies were atypical in FEP during the first 100-300 ms in the right temporoparietal electrodes, along with reduced theta oscillation power. Together, the identified regions represent atypical live face processing systems in early schizophrenia spectrum disorder, which is further correlated with expressive deficits and social withdrawal. The study emphasizes the need for ecologically valid multimodal data acquisition to detect neural hubs crucial in live face processing in early schizophrenia.

papers.title: Extracellular galectin-3 preferentially through CD44 and PD-1 binds activated T cells and marks memory-phenotype T cell subsets.
papers.abstract: Galectin-3 (Gal-3) is a multifunctional β-galactoside-binding lectin implicated in immune regulation, yet its association with T cell phenotypes under physiological and inflammatory conditions remains incompletely defined. We investigated Gal-3 expression and binding on murine and human T cells across developmental stages, tissues, sex, genetic background, circadian time, and inflammatory disease settings. In mice, Gal-3-associated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were dynamically regulated by age, anatomical location, strain, sex, and circadian rhythm. Gal-3+ T cells displayed increased activation markers, enhanced TCR-associated signaling molecules, elevated cytolytic mediators, increased proliferation, and greater apoptosis. Gal-3+ T cells were enriched within central and effector memory compartments and expressed higher levels of co-inhibitory receptors, including PD-1, with ImageStream analysis confirming Gal-3 co-expressed with PD-1. Recombinant Gal-3 preferentially bound activated, but not resting T cells, and associated with CD44 and CD3, suggesting activation-dependent acquisition of extracellular Gal-3. Re-analysis of human thymocyte and Long COVID single-cell RNA-seq datasets further supported an association between LGALS3 expression and activated/exhausted T cell states. Finally, intracellular staining indicated that T cells are unlikely to be a major source of Gal-3. Our findings identify Gal-3 as a context-dependent marker and potential regulator of activated, antigen-experienced T cells, which promotes T cell apoptosis.

papers.title: Optimizing radiation dermatitis management in nasopharyngeal carcinoma patients undergoing radiotherapy: a qualitative study based on patient journey mapping.
papers.abstract: Radiation dermatitis is a common and distressing complication of radiotherapy for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), affecting over 90% of patients. Its clinical management has been widely studied, but patients' evolving needs across the radiotherapy trajectory remain poorly understood. Patient journey mapping can visualize the patient experience and identify care gaps, yet its use in radiation dermatitis management is limited. A descriptive qualitative study used semi-structured interviews with 25 NPC patients undergoing radiotherapy at a tertiary oncology center in China. Purposeful sampling covered four phases: pre-radiotherapy preparation, early radiotherapy, peak radiotherapy, and post-radiotherapy recovery. Data were analyzed using Colaizzi's seven-step method. A patient journey map was developed to visualize tasks, emotions, and pain points at each phase. Sixteen themes emerged across four phases, grouped into tasks, emotions, and pain points. Pre-radiotherapy patients reported anticipatory anxiety, information asymmetry, and fragmented preparation. During early radiotherapy, delayed symptom recognition due to wishful thinking led to missed early intervention. Peak radiotherapy was the nadir, marked by severe wound care difficulties, multidimensional symptom distress (pain, pruritus, sleep disturbance), body image collapse, and social withdrawal. Recovery involved transitional care fragmentation, uncertainty about skin changes, and long-term hyperpigmentation and scarring concerns. The map suggested a "rollercoaster" emotional pattern, with greatest distress at weeks 4-6. Because sampling was cross-sectional across phases, this pattern is an interpretive synthesis, not a demonstrated individual longitudinal trajectory. This study presents one of the first patient journey maps specifically focused on radiation dermatitis management in NPC patients undergoing radiotherapy. It reveals dynamic, phase-specific needs and critical care gaps, including missed opportunities in proactive skin assessment, structured patient education, practical wound care training, and transitional care coordination. The map offers a visual tool to anticipate needs, optimize intervention timing, and design whole-course nursing interventions. Prospective longitudinal studies are needed to validate and refine it for clinical implementation.

papers.title: Uncovering selection bias due to enrollment in Medicare claims studies.
papers.abstract: Research using administrative claims data often excludes individuals with secondary payors or incomplete coverage. We aimed to determine whether doing so leads to selection bias in longitudinal studies of the Medicare population. Using nationally representative data from the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS), we summarized Medicare enrollment trends from 2011 to 2019 and measured the association between self-reported sleep medication use and two outcomes: falls and dementia. There were 8244 Medicare beneficiaries in the NHATS 2011 cohort, and the prevalence of Part C enrollment increased from 29% in 2011 to 42% in 2019. Among those without Part C, the percentage with complete (12 months) Parts A, B, and D coverage increased from 45% in 2011 to 60% in 2019. To assess potential coverage-related selection bias, we repeated discrete-time survey-weighted survival analyses after restricting the cohort by common Medicare enrollment criteria (eg, excluding Part C enrollees). Unadjusted and adjusted associations between sleep medication use and incident dementia or falls were broadly similar across Medicare-defined subsamples and the full cohort. Sleep medication use was not associated with dementia but was positively associated with falls. Sensitivity analyses requiring continuous eligibility showed consistent results. Enrollment in nontraditional Medicare has increased, but these examples did not lead to significant selection bias.
keywords: National Health and Aging Trends Study

papers.title: Non-pharmacological augmentation of trauma-focused psychotherapy for PTSD: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Trauma-focused psychotherapies (TFPs) effectively treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), yet patients show variable response or discontinue treatment. Numerous augmentation strategies have been developed to address these barriers, but the field lacks a framework that extends beyond mechanistic categories as well as a meta-analytic synthesis of their effects. To develop a classification framework for non-pharmacological augmentation strategies of first-line TFP for PTSD and to meta-analytically evaluate whether these strategies improve treatment outcomes. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing TFP augmented with a non-pharmacological intervention versus TFP alone or an active control (i.e. sham intervention or dose increase). Eight databases were searched to July 2026. Augmentation strategies were qualitatively categorised. Primary outcomes were PTSD symptom severity and response rate; dropout was a secondary outcome. Fifty RCTs met inclusion criteria. Their augmentations were categorised within a three-level framework comprising targets, mechanisms, and implementation forms. Of these, 39 trials (40 comparisons; N = 2,853) were meta-analysed and showed no significant overall effects (symptom severity: g = -0.10, p = .062; response: RR = 1.04, p = .111; dropout: RR = 0.94, p = .489). One subgroup targeting sleep disturbance showed an add-on effect. The present findings suggest that augmenting TFP with non-pharmacological interventions does not necessarily lead to incremental efficacy at the overall level, even though small benefits were observed for sleep-focused strategies. Our three-level framework provides a structured approach for conceptualising this heterogeneous field. The absence of a robust overall effect should not be mistaken for evidence that augmentation cannot be effective.

papers.title: Sauna bathing as a health intervention: a qualitative study of personal experiences.
papers.abstract: Sauna bathing has been shown to provide multiple physical and psychological benefits, including reduced cardiovascular risk, pain relief, stress reduction, improved sleep, and enhanced wellbeing. The present study aims to explore sauna bathers' experiences of sauna bathing and consider its potential relevance to health-promoting nursing practice. Using a qualitative, inductive design, the study was conducted in southern Sweden and involved semi-structured interviews with eight participants aged 31-71 years. Data were analysed with a qualitative content analysis. Two main categories and five subcategories emerged. The findings indicate that sauna bathing can alleviate pain, support management of chronic conditions, and promote relaxation and holistic wellbeing. Perceived benefits were influenced by individual preferences and contextual factors. Conclusion: From a Public Health Nurse perspective, sauna bathing may represent an accessible practice with promising implications for health promotion in primary care. Future research should investigate the combined effects of sauna bathing and physical activity to identify possible additive benefits and strengthen the evidence base for integrating sauna use into primary healthcare.

papers.title: Safe Administration of Minimal-to-Moderate Procedural Sedation and Analgesia: Practical Recommendations From the Taiwan Society of Anesthesiologists.
papers.abstract: Procedural sedation exists on a dynamic continuum. Some patients may rapidly and unintentionally progress to deep sedation or general anesthesia. This study is to establish practical recommendations for enhancing patient safety during minimal-to-moderate procedural sedation and analgesia. The key recommendations are as follows: (1) Risk stratification: High-risk patients require careful evaluation and planning by anesthesiologists, particularly those with an American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status ≥ III, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, an anticipated difficult airway, severe cardiovascular disease, advanced age, or organ failure. (2) Pharmacological stewardship: Sedatives and analgesics should be administered incrementally and carefully titrated to clinical effect, with sufficient time between doses. Close vigilance is required when sedatives and opioids are co-administered because of additive respiratory depression. Given its narrow therapeutic window and the potential for rapid, unintended progression to deep sedation, propofol should be restricted to personnel trained in advanced airway rescue. (3) Continuous monitoring: Continuous assessment of consciousness, airway patency, ventilation, oxygenation, and cardiovascular status is essential. Pulse oximetry and cardiovascular monitoring should be routinely performed, while continuous waveform capnography is recommended during moderate sedation to facilitate early detection of hypoventilation or apnea. Personnel must be prepared to provide immediate airway and respiratory rescue when unintended deep sedation occurs. (4) Post-procedural recovery: Following the procedure, patients should undergo structured recovery assessment using validated criteria, including the Modified Aldrete Score and Post-Anesthetic Discharge Scoring System. These findings suggest that standardized risk assessment, careful drug titration, vigilant monitoring, immediate rescue capability, and structured recovery protocols are essential to minimize sedation-related complications and optimize patient safety.

papers.title: Nightly Sleep and Next-Day Physical Activity Structure and Volume: Within-Individual Associations in 81 537 Adults.
papers.abstract: This study examined associations between night-to-night changes in sleep and next-day physical activity structure and volume in 81 537 UK Biobank participants (469 273 night-day observations). Sleep duration, wake after sleep onset, and number of awakenings were related to next-day intensity gradient, mean active-bout duration, activity fragmentation, mean waking-hour acceleration, and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) duration using mixed models that separated within-person deviations from between-person differences and adjusted for 22 covariates. On nights when participants slept longer than their own average, next-day intensity gradient was higher (β = 0.0078, 95% CI 0.0071-0.0085), bouts were longer, fragmentation was lower, and mean waking-hour acceleration was higher, while MVPA duration was shorter (β = -0.0681, 95% CI -0.0753 to -0.0609). Spline models suggested outcome-specific departures from linearity. In multi-lag models, associations with structure outcomes remained statistically significant for sleep deviations three nights earlier (lag 2), whereas those with volume outcomes did not. These observational findings show that activity volume and structure can exhibit different day-to-day associations with sleep.
papers.journal: Scandinavian journal of medicine & science in sports

papers.title: Sleep-Deprivation Serum Induces Mitochondrial Stress in BV2 Cells: Responses to P2Y12-Targeted Pharmacological Modulation.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) disrupts neuroimmune and metabolic homeostasis, but whether circulating factors generated after sleep loss alter microglial responses to purinergic pharmacological modulation remains unclear. P2Y12 is a microglia-enriched purinergic receptor that regulates process dynamics, calcium signaling, and microglial interactions with neurons and vascular-glial interfaces. Here, we established an in vitro serum-transfer model to test whether serum from sleep-deprived mice alters mitochondrial and Rhod-2 fluorescence responses to P2Y12-targeted compounds in BV2 cells. Mice were subjected to forced-wheel SD consisting of one wheel revolution every 2 s for 4 h per day over 4 consecutive days, and serum was obtained by cardiac blood collection followed by centrifugation. BV2 cells were treated with control or SD serum in the absence or presence of the P2Y12 antagonist MRS2395 or the P2Y12 agonist 2-MeSADP. Mitochondrial membrane potential was assessed by JC-1 red/green ratio imaging, mitochondrial network integrity by MitoTracker-based segmentation and skeletonization, and Rhod-2 fluorescence responses by single-cell F/F0 imaging. SD serum decreased the JC-1 ratio, increased maximal depolarization, reduced mitochondrial skeleton length and mitochondrial area fraction, and suppressed Rhod-2 responses. Under control-serum conditions, MRS2395 markedly enhanced Rhod-2 responses, whereas the increase in the area under the Rhod-2 response curve with 2-MeSADP was not significant after Holm correction. Under SD-serum conditions, however, neither compound consistently restored the mitochondrial or Rhod-2 response profile. Together, these findings link SD-serum exposure to mitochondrial impairment and attenuated Rhod-2 fluorescence responses in BV2 cells, and suggest that serum context may influence cellular responses to P2Y12-targeted compounds.
papers.journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology

papers.title: Tracking Neurophysiological Trajectories in Adolescent Non-Suicidal Self-Injury During Mindfulness-Based Intervention: A Longitudinal Single-Channel EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Adolescent non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) remains a major clinical challenge, and objective neurophysiological monitoring during early intervention is lacking. This prospective longitudinal observational study characterized longitudinal EEG trajectories during an individualized home-based EEG biofeedback editation (H-EBM) intervention in hospitalized adolescents with NSSI and explored whether neurophysiological trajectory features were associated with emotional improvement. Fifty-two hospitalized adolescents with NSSI (DSM-5 criteria) who received routine inpatient psychiatric care together with daily H-EBM sessions over approximately 10 days were included in the per-protocol analysis. H-EBM integrated metaphor-guided therapeutic narratives with real-time EEG biofeedback via a single-lead device (Fp1, 512 Hz). Emotional states were assessed at admission and discharge using the profile of mood states (POMS). Participants were exploratorily classified into exploratory responder ( n = 36 ) and non-responder ( n = 16 ) subgroups based on total mood disturbance (TMD) improvement. Longitudinal alpha/beta power ratio trajectories were compared between subgroups, and associations between EEG trajectory slopes and TMD improvement were examined. The exploratory responder subgroup showed significant reductions in TMD scores and core symptom subscales (depression and tension; all p < 0.001 ), whereas the exploratory non-responder subgroup showed no improvement. The alpha/beta ratio in the exploratory responder subgroup exhibited a progressive upward trajectory across training sessions, while this ratio remained stable or fluctuated in the exploratory non-responder subgroup. The alpha/beta ratio slope was positively associated with TMD improvement scores (Pearson r = 0.43 , 95% CI [0.18, 0.63], p = 0.002 ). Exploratory logistic regression suggested that the alpha/beta ratio slope was associated with exploratory responder status after adjusting for age and gender (OR = 9.49, 95% CI [1.01, 89.44], p = 0.049 ). Exploratory ROC analysis showed moderate apparent (in-sample) discriminative performance (AUC = 0.774, 95% CI [0.638, 0.899]). Longitudinal neurophysiological trajectories during individualized H-EBM were associated with emotional improvement in hospitalized adolescents with NSSI. These preliminary findings suggest that EEG trajectory analysis may represent a promising objective monitoring approach during individualized mindfulness-based interventions. Given the observational design without a control group, future randomized controlled studies are warranted to examine potential therapeutic effects.

papers.title: Investigating the Causal Relationship and Shared Genetic Basis Between Multisite Chronic Pain and Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: Chronic pain is a prevalent and disabling condition with substantial personal and societal impact. Multisite chronic pain (MCP), defined as chronic pain across multiple body sites, is a more severe phenotype that commonly co-occurs with sleep disorders, particularly sleep apnea (SA), yet their causal and shared genetic basis remains unclear. We performed an integrative genetic analysis using large-scale GWAS data, combining Mendelian randomization (MR), MiXeR, and conjunctional false discovery rate (conjFDR) approaches. MR supported a bidirectional causal relationship between MCP and SA, with a substantially stronger effect of MCP on SA than the reverse direction (MCP to SA: OR = 1.54, p = 1.45 × 10-3; SA to MCP: β = 0.033, p = 1.60 × 10-2). MiXeR revealed extensive polygenic overlap between MCP and SA, with a Dice coefficient of 0.617. ConjFDR identified 62 shared loci, with mapped genes enriched in brain-related pathways. MCP and SA show bidirectional causal effects, with a stronger effect in the MCP to SA direction, and substantial shared genetic architecture. These findings provide insights into the genetic basis of MCP-SA comorbidity and may inform its prevention and management.

papers.title: Precipitants of and Immediate Staff Responses to Violence from Older People With Dementia and/or Delirium in Hospitals.
papers.abstract: To explore precipitants of reported workplace violence involving older hospital patients with dementia and/or delirium and staff's immediate responses. A retrospective qualitative analysis of incident reports. A stratified random sample was extracted from 206,144 workplace violence incident reports recorded between 2018 and 2022 in a 5-hospital metropolitan health service's incident reporting system. A total of 184 reports involving 91 older people with dementia and/or delirium in hospitals were included. Within a social constructivist paradigm, conventional content analysis was used to analyse free-text descriptions contained in staff incident reports. Three broad categories of precipitants were identified: (1) patient-related precipitants, including pain, sleep disturbance and confusion; (2) clinical-care-related precipitants, involving reactions to personal care delivery or medication administration, dissatisfaction with the care and/or services received, resistance to care, miscommunication and reactions to staff attempts to constrain and/or redirect for safety; (3) psychosocial-environmental-related precipitants, involving other patients' verbal abuse or threatening behaviours and other patients stopping the patient's intrusive behaviours. Staff immediate responses included agitation and pain assessment, verbal assurance, redirection or de-escalation, seeking urgent clinical and/or safety team assistance, physically restrictive practices, analgesic or sedative medications and environmental modifications. The precipitants to reported workplace violence regarding older people with dementia and/or delirium in hospitals were phenomenologically similar to the precipitants to aggression described among people with dementia and/or delirium in the literature. Generic workforce violence management strategies were commonly reported, which may limit clinicians' meaningful interpretation of behaviours in people with dementia and/or delirium. More focused behaviour identification and management strategies to manage violence involving older people with dementia and/or delirium are required because generic workplace violence approaches may overlook underlying causes, contributing to inappropriate behaviour management. What problem did the study address? The study advances our understanding of precipitants of and immediate staff responses to violence incidents involving older people with dementia and/or delirium in hospitals. What were the main findings? The study found that reported violence from older people with dementia and/or delirium in hospitals encompasses diagnosis-related precipitants of aggression. Staff predominantly reported applying generic violence-management strategies rather than diagnosis-specific strategies. Where and on whom will the research have an impact? The research findings have a significant impact on healthcare professionals and policymakers in Australia regarding healthcare provision for older people with dementia in hospitals. The findings may also have significant impacts on other relevant international contexts. The CASP Qualitative Studies Checklist was used to guide the writing of the study report (Critical Appraisal Skills Programme, 2024). The Evaluating Quality Care Patient and Carer Advisory Board provided advice and feedback on the initial concept for this study. The manuscript was reviewed and approved by the data custodian prior to submission for publication consideration. WHAT DOES THIS PAPER CONTRIBUTE TO THE WIDER GLOBAL CLINICAL COMMUNITY?: The study improves our knowledge of the precipitants of and immediate staff responses to violence from older people with dementia and/or delirium in hospitals. This paper provided evidence to support that more focused behaviour identification and management strategies are required to manage violence involving older people with dementia and/or delirium in hospitals.

papers.title: Seasonal and daily rhythms in healthy adults and individuals with obesity: associations with selected hormones and lifestyle factors.
papers.abstract: Biological timing systems, including circadian and seasonal rhythms, play a key role in regulating human physiology. The central circadian "body clock," located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, coordinates daily rhythms both centrally and via peripheral clocks in metabolic tissues. Seasonal rhythms, in turn, are shaped by environmental cues such as photoperiod and temperature and may influence mood, appetite, sleep, physical activity, hormonal secretion, and thermoregulation. Although seasonal responses are generally weaker in humans than in many other animals, evidence suggests that some physiological processes remain seasonally regulated. From a physiological anthropology perspective, these rhythms can be viewed as adaptive mechanisms that align human physiology and behavior with predictable environmental changes. These timing systems are increasingly recognized as important regulators of metabolic homeostasis. Disruption of circadian and seasonal rhythms may contribute to insulin resistance, altered energy expenditure, fat accumulation, and obesity-related dysfunction. Human studies suggest that biological timing is reflected in chronotype-related behaviors, endocrine responses, seasonal hormonal variation, and thermoregulatory adaptation. Obesity is a complex, multifactorial disease that cannot be explained solely by excessive energy intake and low physical activity. It develops through interactions between external factors, such as an unhealthy diet and a sedentary lifestyle, and internal factors, including genetic, metabolic, endocrine, and behavioral mechanisms. Therefore, obesity should be understood not only as a disorder of energy balance but also as a condition influenced by disrupted biological timing. This article builds on our 2015 review (Kanikowska et al., Int J Biometeorol 59:377-84, 2015) by synthesizing recent literature and emerging perspectives on the roles of circadian and seasonal rhythms in obesity.

papers.title: Resting-state EEG features of cognitive fluctuations across the Lewy body disease spectrum.
papers.abstract: Cognitive fluctuations (CF) are a core feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) that negatively impact quality of life. Despite their prevalence and negative impact, CF are challenging to identify clinically. The goal of this study was to identify easily obtainable EEG features associated with CF across the spectrum of Lewy body disease (LB). We conducted a cross-sectional study of 53 patients prospectively enrolled through the outpatient clinics of the Department of Neurology at Virginia Commonwealth University. Based on the Clinician Assessment of Fluctuations, participants were categorized as LB disease without CF (LB-CF) or LB disease with CF (LB + CF). All participants underwent a resting-state EEG recording with eyes closed for at least 3 min. EEG data were preprocessed and the following features were extracted: dominant frequency (DF), dominant frequency variability (DFV), dominant frequency prevalence (DFP), and individual alpha peak frequency (IAF). We applied Kruskal-Wallis tests and logistic regression models to evaluate differences in EEG features between study groups. We analyzed EEG features for 29 LB + CF and 24 LB-CF participants. Compared to the LB-CF group, the LB + CF group had significantly lower DF, DFP-alpha, and IAF in all derivations (all p < 0.05). In logistic regression analysis adjusting for age, sex, and MoCA score, these EEG features remained significant predictors of group (LB + CF vs. LB-CF, all q < 0.05). The elastic-net logistic regression model identified five predictors (anterior DFP-alpha, anterior DFP-pre-alpha, anterior DF, temporal DF, and temporal IAF) achieving an AUC of 0.86, whereas anterior DFP-alpha alone achieved an AUC of 0.85. Among patients with LB disease, resting-state EEG features were associated with CF and were significant predictors of CF even after adjustment for age, sex, and MoCA. The development of an EEG-based biomarker of CF using this set of features could improve diagnosis of Lewy body dementia.

papers.title: Diabetes and all-cause mortality in a national telemonitored heart failure cohort: role of comorbidities, heart failure etiology burden, and short-term weight variability.
papers.abstract: Diabetes mellitus is common in patients with heart failure (HF) and is associated with worse outcomes. However, its prognostic role in real-world telemonitored HF populations remains insufficiently characterized. We evaluated the association between diabetes and all-cause mortality in a national telemonitored HF cohort while considering HF severity, comorbidities, HF etiology burden, and short-term weight variability (WV). We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults enrolled in the French Satelia® Cardio telemonitoring program between 2018 and 2024 (NCT07561866). Baseline clinical characteristics, HF etiologies, comorbidities, and repeated weight measurements were analyzed. Short-term WV was defined as the mean absolute 10-day weight change per patient and categorized according to the cohort median. Survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analyses and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models. Among 16,556 patients (mean age 74.9 ± 12.9 years; 64% male), 4,723 (28.5%) had diabetes. Median follow-up was 13 months in patients with diabetes and 11 months in those without diabetes; 2,266 patients died (13.7%). Patients with diabetes more frequently had ischemic and hypertensive HF etiologies, obesity and greater HF etiology burden. In multivariable models without NYHA class, diabetes was independently associated with higher mortality, with a significant diabetes-by-age interaction suggesting a stronger association among patients aged < 75 years. After adjustment for NYHA class in the smaller subgroup, this association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant. Male sex, clinician-reported renal failure, combined chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and sleep apnea syndrome, and higher NYHA class were associated with higher mortality, whereas obesity was associated with lower mortality. Individual HF etiologies were not consistently associated with mortality across adjusted models, whereas increasing HF etiology burden remained associated with higher mortality. High short-term WV was associated with poorer survival. In this large national telemonitored HF cohort, the association between diabetes and mortality was attenuated after accounting for HF severity assessed by NYHA class. Mortality was more consistently associated with HF severity, comorbidities and cumulative HF etiology burden than with individual HF etiologies. Short-term WV emerged as an exploratory telemonitoring-derived marker associated with poorer survival. These findings support a multidimensional approach to risk assessment in patients with diabetes.
